Abstract\\r\\nReliable and bandwidth-efficient wireless transmission of navigation-relevant information is a core requirement for autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operation over noisy and fading wireless links. Conventional digital communication systems and reconstruction-oriented Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (DeepJSCC) schemes are optimized to recover the transmitted signal with minimum distortion, independent of how that signal will subsequently be used. This project investigates a Task-Oriented DeepJSCC communication system in which the encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end to directly optimize UAV navigation (goal-reaching) performance rather than reconstruction fidelity.\\r\\nA compact UAV kinematic state representation, comprising position, velocity, and goal-relative information, is transmitted over Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading channels and used by a UAV navigation controller operating on a simplified two-dimensional kinematic model. The Task-Oriented DeepJSCC system is benchmarked against a conventional digital communication baseline and a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC baseline under matched channel, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and bandwidth conditions. The project is entirely simulation-based, implemented in Python/PyTorch, and does not involve physical UAV hardware, software-defined radios, or real flight tests.\\r\\nA structured literature verification (Section 7) confirms that task-oriented and semantic communication has already been investigated for UAV command-and-control transmission, UAV swarm tracking control, and UAV vision-based localization, and that task-oriented DeepJSCC trained directly against a closed-loop control objective has been demonstrated for autonomous driving. The specific combination targeted here � a DeepJSCC encoder/decoder trained on a UAV navigation/goal-reaching objective, operating on a low-dimensional kinematic state rather than imagery, and systematically evaluated under both AWGN and Rayleigh fading against conventional and reconstruction-oriented baselines � has not been reported in the reviewed literature and forms the focus of this Final Year Project. The expected outcome is an empirically grounded characterization of when, and by how much, task-oriented optimization improves UAV navigation robustness relative to conventional and reconstruction-oriented alternatives under wireless channel impairments.\\r\\n3. Introduction\\r\\nSmall, low-power unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used for surveillance, delivery, inspection, and search-and-rescue missions, in architectures where the UAV depends on a wireless link to a ground station or remote controller for navigation-relevant information exchange. This link is rarely ideal: it is subject to additive thermal noise, and, because UAVs move through space with time-varying line-of-sight conditions and multipath reflections from terrain, buildings, or foliage, it is also subject to small-scale fading. Under such impairments, conventional bit-level communication pipelines, which separate source compression from channel coding and aim to reconstruct the transmitted signal exactly, are known to suffer from the so-called \\\"cliff effect\\\": performance degrades gracefully until the channel SNR falls below the design threshold, after which the system fails abruptly (Bourtsoulatze, Kurka & G�nd�z, 2019).\\r\\nDeep Joint Source-Channel Coding (DeepJSCC) replaces the separate source and channel coding stages with a pair of jointly trained neural networks that map source symbols directly to complex-valued channel input symbols, and has been shown both under AWGN and slow Rayleigh fading to degrade gracefully rather than catastrophically as SNR deteriorates (Bourtsoulatze, Kurka & G�nd�z, 2019). The great majority of DeepJSCC research, however, is reconstruction-oriented: the encoder and decoder are trained to minimize a distortion metric between the transmitted and received signal, independent of what the received information will subsequently be used for. In parallel, a body of work on task-oriented and goal-oriented communication argues that when the purpose of transmission is a downstream decision or control action, the communication system should instead be optimized directly against that downstream task's performance rather than against signal fidelity (G�nd�z et al., 2023; Shao, Mao & Zhang, 2022).\\r\\nThis project investigates the intersection of these two ideas for a specific and practically relevant downstream task: UAV navigation toward a goal position. It asks whether training a DeepJSCC encoder/decoder pair directly on navigation/goal-reaching performance, rather than on reconstruction error, yields a communication system that is more robust to wireless channel impairments in the sense that matters to the mission � reaching the goal � even if it is not necessarily better at reproducing the original navigation state bit-for-bit.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n4. Background\\r\\n2.1 Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding\\r\\nClassical digital communication systems follow Shannon's source-channel separation principle: a source coder compresses the data and a channel coder adds redundancy for error protection, with the two designed independently. While asymptotically optimal for point-to-point channels with unbounded blocklength, separation-based systems are known to perform poorly at short blocklengths and to fail abruptly when the operating SNR drops below the design point. DeepJSCC instead parameterizes the encoder and decoder as convolutional or transformer-based neural networks trained end-to-end as an autoencoder, with a non-trainable channel layer inserted between them to model the wireless channel (Bourtsoulatze, Kurka & G�nd�z, 2019). Subsequent work has extended DeepJSCC with attention modules for content-adaptive coding (Xu et al., 2022), bandwidth-agile and variable-rate transmission (Kurka & G�nd�z, 2021), and explicit multipath/fading and MIMO channel models (Yang, Bian & Kim, 2022; Wu et al., 2024).\\r\\n2.2 Semantic, Goal-Oriented, and Task-Oriented Communication\\r\\nThe terms semantic communication, goal-oriented communication, and task-oriented communication are often used loosely in the literature; this proposal adopts the distinctions summarized in G�nd�z et al. (2023). Semantic communication is concerned with conveying the meaning of a message rather than its exact bit sequence, typically evaluated by a semantic-level similarity measure. Goal-oriented communication extends this by explicitly tying the value of transmitted information to a specific goal or action to be taken by the receiver, often using metrics such as the age of information (AoI) or value of information (VoI). Task-oriented communication, the framing adopted in this project, specifically optimizes the communication system � encoder, and where relevant the decoder and downstream model � against the performance of a defined downstream inference or control task, commonly formalized through an information bottleneck (IB) objective that trades off representation compactness against task-relevant informativeness (Shao, Mao & Zhang, 2022).\\r\\nA Task-Oriented DeepJSCC system, as investigated in this project, combines both ideas: it uses the DeepJSCC architecture (a jointly trained neural encoder/decoder mapping directly to channel symbols, without explicit source/channel separation) but replaces the reconstruction-based training objective with a task-oriented loss defined on the downstream task's performance.\\r\\n2.3 UAV Wireless Communication Challenges\\r\\nUAV communication links differ from static or slowly moving terrestrial links in that the channel can vary rapidly due to the UAV's own motion, altitude changes, and antenna orientation, producing time-varying multipath and Doppler effects. Bandwidth is also often constrained by regulatory allocation and by the need to share spectrum with other aerial or ground users. These characteristics motivate the choice of AWGN and Rayleigh fading as the two channel models investigated in this project: AWGN represents a noise-limited baseline case, while Rayleigh fading represents a non-line-of-sight, richly scattering environment representative of low-altitude urban or cluttered operation.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\n[read_files: showing lines 1-40 of 295. The files are untouched; start what you still need again rather than assuming it survived.\\n</since_your_last_turn>\\n\\nThis research is trying to figure out the best way to send information from a drone to itself (or to a controller) over a noisy, unreliable radio link so the drone can still navigate to a target. Normally, when you send data over a bad connection, you first compress it, then add error-correction bits, then transmit—and if some bits get corrupted, the drone's position estimate goes wrong and it crashes or misses the goal. This project instead tests a smarter approach called \\\"task-oriented joint source-channel coding,\\\" where a neural network learns to encode the drone's state (position, velocity, goal) directly into radio symbols in a way that's optimized not for perfect reconstruction of the data, but for the actual task—reaching the goal. They compare three methods: (1) a traditional digital baseline that quantizes, adds convolutional codes, and uses QPSK (the \\\"old-school\\\" way), (2) a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC that tries to faithfully rebuild the drone's state at the receiver, and (3) a task-oriented DeepJSCC that skips caring about perfect reconstruction and directly minimizes navigation error. They test all three under different bandwidths (how many radio symbols you're allowed to use per state update) and different noise levels, in both clean AWGN channels and fading Rayleigh channels. The surprising finding is that the fancy task-oriented neural approach actually does worse than plain reconstruction at low bandwidth, and the traditional digital method wins big once you give it enough bandwidth—so the \\\"task-oriented\\\" idea isn't automatically better; it depends on how much radio spectrum you have. The whole thing is built as a rigorous, reproducible experiment with frozen settings, multiple random seeds, and proper statistics, so the comparisons are fair and not cherry-picked.\\n\\n Mam Ismat: Novelty pr question hai\\n Mam Ismat: Or research question mein msla hai\\n Mam Ismat: UAV khud ko hi message send kr ra\\n\\nmam ka view hai\"}],\"tags\":[\"USER_PROMPT\"],\"sentAt\":1791779318114,\"keepDuringTruncation\":true}],\"stepsRemaining\":200,\"creditsUsed\":0,\"directCreditsUsed\":0,\"systemPrompt\":\"You are Buffy, the coding agent behind Codebuff. ARCHITECTURE (exact tensor shapes)\\n\\nB = batch. Task-oriented training path (eval is identical under `no_grad`):\\n\\n```\\ns_t              [B,6]   raw physical state\\ns̄_t = norm(s_t)  [B,6]   per-component affine, clip to [−1,1]\\n\\nENCODER   Linear(6,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,2k)\\na_t              [B,2k]\\nz̃_R = a_t[:, :k] , z̃_I = a_t[:, k:2k]        (stacked I/Q convention, fixed)\\nz̃_t              [B,k]   complex, k channel uses, ρ = k/6\\n\\nPOWER NORM  z_t = √(kP) · z̃_t / √(Σ_i |z̃_t,i|² + ε)     [B,k]  per-codeword\\n\\nCHANNEL (AWGN)      y_t = z_t + n_t ,  n ~ CN(0, σ²I)     [B,k]\\nCHANNEL (Rayleigh)  h_t [B,1] ~ CN(0,1) per codeword; y_t = h_t·z_t + n_t\\nEQUALIZE            ỹ_t = y_t · h* / max(|h|², ε_h)       [B,k]\\nTO REAL             [Re ỹ ; Im ỹ]                          [B,2k]\\n\\nDECODER   Linear(2k,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,6)\\nŝ̄_t              [B,6]\\nŝ_t = denorm(ŝ̄_t) [B,6]\\n\\nCONTROLLER  e_t = ŝ_t[:,0:2] − ŝ_t[:,4:6]\\n            u*_t = −Kp·e_t − Kv·ŝ_t[:,2:4]\\n            u_t = clip(u*_t, −u_max, u_max)               [B,2]\\n\\nDYNAMICS    p_{t+1} = p_t + Δt·v_t + ½Δt²·u_t             [B,2]\\n            v_{t+1} = v_clip(v_t + Δt·u_t, v_max)          [B,2]\\n            s_{t+1} = [p_{t+1} ; v_{t+1} ; p_g]            [B,6]\\n\\nloop t = 0 … T−1 ; losses Ld, Lu, Lv, LT (scalars) accumulate\\n```\\n\\nDigital chain (same normalization, controller, dynamics, channel):\\n\\n```\\ns̄_t [B,6] → uniform scalar quantize (B bits/comp) → indices [B,6] → bits [B,6B]\\n→ conv encode → coded bits [B, N_coded],  N_coded = 6B/R_c\\n→ Gray map → symbols z_t [B, n_dig],  n_dig = N_coded/log2(M)\\n→ same channel → equalize → LLRs [B, N_coded] → Viterbi → b̂ → dequantize → ŝ̄_t [B,6]\\n→ same controller → same dynamics\\n```\\n\\nBudget identity enforced at config time: **6B = k·R_c·log2(M)** (see A1).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. CHANNEL VERIFICATION\\n\\nEach item states the check the implementation must pass before it is trusted.\\n\\n1. **Complex representation.** z̃_i = a_i + j·a_{k+i} (stacked). k complex uses; 2k is only the real width of the final linear layer. Assert: encoder output reinterpreted to [B,k] complex; config sanity print ρ = k/6. The decoder input width is 2k.\\n2. **Power normalization.** Per-codeword: after normalization, (1/k)Σ_i|z_i|² = P·(1 + O(ε)) — exact per sample, not merely on batch average. Individual symbols may have unequal energies (expected). Guard: ε only prevents division by ~0; verify ε ≪ typical ‖z̃‖² so it never reshapes the distribution.\\n3. **AWGN variance.** σ² = P·10^(−SNR_dB/10); sample n_R, n_I ~ N(0, σ²/2) each so E|n|² = σ². Empirical test: 10⁶ samples, mean |n|² within 0.1% of σ². The classic bug (σ² per I/Q component) produces a systematic 3 dB SNR shift — detectable by matching the simulated Gray-QPSK BER to Q(√(E_s/N₀)) at fixed SNRs (textbook closed form used **only** to validate the simulator, not as a baseline).\\n4. **Rayleigh fading.** h_R, h_I ~ N(0, 1/2) ⇒ E|h|² = 1, |h| Rayleigh, phase uniform. One scalar h per codeword: h has shape [B,1], broadcast over the k symbols; a fresh h per state transmission. Empirical tests: histogram vs Rayleigh pdf; E|h|² ≈ 1; within-codeword symbol correlation = 1 (block), across codewords ≈ 0 (rejects the per-symbol fast-fading bug).\\n5. **CSI / equalization.** Perfect CSIR; ỹ = y·h*/max(|h|², ε_h) ≡ y/h for |h|² ≫ ε_h. After equalization the per-codeword SNR is |h|²P/σ² (instantaneous, heavy-tailed); the config SNR axis is the **average** SNR = P/σ² since E|h|² = 1. The identical equalizer is applied in the digital baseline. The guard keeps training gradients finite when |h| → 0.\\n6. **SNR calculation & bandwidth ratio.** One function `snr_db → σ²` is the single source of truth for every method; no per-method recomputation, no E_b/N₀ on the comparison axis (digital-only supplementary label). Runtime asserts: ρ = k/6 with integer k, and n_dig == k for the digital chain (misconfiguration fails loudly rather than silently changing the budget).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. FAIRNESS CHECK\\n\\n- **Single shared implementations** (not copies) of: dynamics, controller, normalization, channel models, equalizer, episode/RNG pipeline, metrics. A method can only differ in its encoder/quantizer → decoder/dequantizer map and its training objective.\\n- **Identical for all three methods:** 6-D state; dynamics and limits; goal and success criterion; test episodes (same start/goal per episode index, frozen seeds); paired channel realizations (same n and h per episode/step); SNR grid and definition (P/σ² per complex symbol); P = 1; budget n_dig == k (asserted); 1 transmission per control step; perfect CSIR + ZF equalization; controller gains and clipping; horizon and metrics.\\n- **Legitimately different (the independent variable):** how the state is mapped to channel symbols and back, and the training objective. The digital baseline may carry fewer effective source bits at matched k — that is a *result* (bandwidth-limited separation starves), not an unfairness, provided the budget equality holds and its configuration is reported.\\n- **Guard rails in code:** runtime asserts (budget equality, shapes, identical seeds); an \\\"oracle perfect-state, no channel\\\" run allowed only as a clearly labeled upper reference, never a fourth comparator; normalization ranges from config only; no statistic ever computed on test data; digital BER/BLER reported as link diagnostics, never substituted for task metrics.\\n\\n**Decision A1 (digital budget), restated with options:**\\n- **Option A — fit bits to budget:** for each ρ, choose (B, R_c, M) with 6B = k·R_c·log2(M), best feasible. Example feasible exact fits: k=3: uncoded 256-QAM → B=4 (≈1.07 m position quantization); uncoded 64-QAM → B=3; conv R_c=1/2 + 256-QAM → B=2. k=2: uncoded 64-QAM → B=2. k=1: B=1 at best — navigation-degenerate. Strictly matched, but the digital baseline is quantization-starved at ρ ≤ 1/2.\\n- **Option B — scale budget to payload:** fix B = 8 (48 source bits), give the digital chain n_dig = ⌈48/(R_c·log2 M)⌉ symbols (e.g., 24 uncoded 256-QAM symbols, ρ_dig = 4; or 48 QPSK symbols with R_c = 1/2, ρ_dig = 8), and report its true bandwidth ratio alongside. Your protocol doc itself sketches this direction (16-bit example → k = 48).\\n- **Recommendation:** run the main matrix at the frozen ρ ∈ {1/6, 1/3, 1/2} with Option-A digital configurations (fair at equal k, expected to fail — a genuine finding), **plus** Option-B digital reference curves clearly labeled with their larger ρ. This keeps budget-matched honesty and still shows what separated design achieves when given enough bandwidth. Your sign-off required.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 6. IMPLEMENTATION RISKS (ways this could silently become mathematically inconsistent)\\n\\n1. **I/Q variance factor-2 bug** — sampling n_R, n_I with variance σ² instead of σ²/2 shifts every SNR by 3 dB. Mitigation: the §4.3 empirical test.\\n2. **Channel-use miscounting** — treating 2k real outputs as 2k uses, or letting the digital chain use n_dig ≠ k without asserting it. Mitigation: runtime asserts + config sanity print.\\n3. **Wrong normalization granularity** — per-symbol or per-batch power normalization instead of per-codeword changes the SNR semantics. Mitigation: per-sample check that (1/k)Σ|z_i|² = P.\\n4. **Fast vs block fading** — drawing h per symbol instead of per codeword destroys the slow-fading comparison. Mitigation: h shape [B,1] and the correlation test in §4.4.\\n5. **Asymmetric CSI** — equalizing one method and not another, or ε_h applied in only some paths. Mitigation: one shared equalizer module.\\n6. **SNR-axis drift for digital** — quoting E_b/N₀ for the coded/modulated chain against E_s/N₀ for DeepJSCC. Mitigation: single σ² source of truth; E_b/N₀ only as a label.\\n7. **Normalization leakage or drift** — ranges computed from data, or different clip behavior between train and eval; denormalization using unclipped bounds. Mitigation: constants in config, one pair of functions used everywhere.\\n8. **Controller information leak** — feeding any ground-truth quantity (e.g., true goal or true position) to one method's controller. Every controller input must come from that method's received representation. Mitigation: controller consumes only the decoded/denormalized state tensor.\\n9. **Autograd pitfalls in the rollout** — detaching z or h, or clipping away all gradient (dead zones at saturation are physically correct but must be understood); noise/h must enter as constants (leaves), while gradients flow through z, decoder, encoder. Mitigation: gradient-flow unit test (loss.backward reaches encoder weights).\\n10. **Loss off-by-one** — Ld/Lv summed over the wrong index range, Lu including t = T, or LT evaluated at T−1. Mitigation: implement exactly as §1.1 row 12; one shared loss used for both training and reporting.\\n11. **Success/failure semantics mismatch** — ∃t vs terminal-only success, and inconsistent boundary-exit handling between training and eval. Mitigation: A4/A5 frozen in config; one episode-termination module.\\n12. **Digital strawman or capacity ghost** — accidentally giving the digital chain capacity-achieving performance, or crippling it via a coarse quantizer without reporting the budget arithmetic. Mitigation: Option A/B reporting rules; textbook BER-curve validation of the implemented modem.\\n13. **RNG contamination** — one global seed reused across episode generation, init, shuffling, and noise breaks paired evaluation. Mitigation: dedicated `torch.Generator` per purpose; test noise/h regenerated identically per (episode, step) for every method.\\n14. **Quantizer/normalization mismatch** — quantizing with a different range or step convention than the dequantizer assumes, or forgetting the clip before dequantization. Mitigation: quantize/dequantize round-trip unit test (error ≤ Δ/2 noiseless).\\n15. **Velocity handling asymmetry** — v_max enforced in one method's loop but not another's. Mitigation: clip inside the shared dynamics module (A3).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 7. ARCHITECTURE (exact tensor shapes)\\n+\\n+B = batch. Task-oriented training path (eval is identical under `no_grad`):\\n+\\n+```\\n+s_t              [B,6]   raw physical state\\n+s̄_t = norm(s_t)  [B,6]   per-component affine, clip to [−1,1]\\n+\\n+ENCODER   Linear(6,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,2k)\\n+a_t              [B,2k]\\n+z̃_R = a_t[:, :k] , z̃_I = a_t[:, k:2k]        (stacked I/Q convention, fixed)\\n+z̃_t              [B,k]   complex, k channel uses, ρ = k/6\\n+\\n+POWER NORM  z_t = √(kP) · z̃_t / √(Σ_i |z̃_t,i|² + ε)     [B,k]  per-codeword\\n+\\n+CHANNEL (AWGN)      y_t = z_t + n_t ,  n ~ CN(0, σ²I)     [B,k]\\n+CHANNEL (Rayleigh)  h_t [B,1] ~ CN(0,1) per codeword; y_t = h_t·z_t + n_t\\n+EQUALIZE            ỹ_t = y_t · h* / max(|h|², ε_h)       [B,k]\\n+TO REAL             [Re ỹ ; Im ỹ]                          [B,2k]\\n+\\n+DECODER   Linear(2k,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,128) → PReLU → Linear(128,6)\\n+ŝ̄_t              [B,6]\\n+ŝ_t = denorm(ŝ̄_t) [B,6]\\n+\\n+CONTROLLER  e_t = ŝ_t[:,0:2] − ŝ_t[:,4:6]\\n+            u*_t = −Kp·e_t − Kv·ŝ_t[:,2:4]\\n+            u_t = clip(u*_t, −u_max, u_max)               [B,2]\\n+\\n+DYNAMICS    p_{t+1} = p_t + Δt·v_t + ½Δt²·u_t             [B,2]\\n+            v_{t+1} = v_clip(v_t + Δt·u_t, v_max)          [B,2]\\n+            s_{t+1} = [p_{t+1} ; v_{t+1} ; p_g]            [B,6]\\n+\\n+loop t = 0 … T−1 ; losses Ld, Lu, Lv, LT (scalars) accumulate\\n+```\\n+\\n+Digital chain (same normalization, controller, dynamics, channel):\\n+\\n+```\\n+s̄_t [B,6] → uniform scalar quantize (B bits/comp) → indices [B,6] → bits [B,6B]\\n+→ conv encode → coded bits [B, N_coded],  N_coded = 6B/R_c\\n+→ Gray map → symbols z_t [B, n_dig],  n_dig = N_coded/log2(M)\\n+→ same channel → equalize → LLRs [B, N_coded] → Viterbi → b̂ → dequantize → ŝ̄_t [B,6]\\n+→ same controller → same dynamics\\n+```\\n+\\n+Budget identity enforced at config time: **6B = k·R_c·log2(M)** (see A1).\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 4. CHANNEL VERIFICATION\\n+\\n+Each item states the check the implementation must pass before it is trusted.\\n+\\n+1. **Complex representation.** z̃_i = a_i + j·a_{k+i} (stacked). k complex uses; 2k is only the real width of the final linear layer. Assert: encoder output reinterpreted to [B,k] complex; config sanity print ρ = k/6. The decoder input width is 2k.\\n+2. **Power normalization.** Per-codeword: after normalization, (1/k)Σ_i|z_i|² = P·(1 + O(ε)) — exact per sample, not merely on batch average. Individual symbols may have unequal energies (expected). Guard: ε only prevents division by ~0; verify ε ≪ typical ‖z̃‖² so it never reshapes the distribution.\\n+3. **AWGN variance.** σ² = P·10^(−SNR_dB/10); sample n_R, n_I ~ N(0, σ²/2) each so E|n|² = σ². Empirical test: 10⁶ samples, mean |n|² within 0.1% of σ². The classic bug (σ² per I/Q component) produces a systematic 3 dB SNR shift — detectable by matching the simulated Gray-QPSK BER to Q(√(E_s/N₀)) at fixed SNRs (textbook closed form used **only** to validate the simulator, not as a baseline).\\n+4. **Rayleigh fading.** h_R, h_I ~ N(0, 1/2) ⇒ E|h|² = 1, |h| Rayleigh, phase uniform. One scalar h per codeword: h has shape [B,1], broadcast over the k symbols; a fresh h per state transmission. Empirical tests: histogram vs Rayleigh pdf; E|h|² ≈ 1; within-codeword symbol correlation = 1 (block), across codewords ≈ 0 (rejects the per-symbol fast-fading bug).\\n+5. **CSI / equalization.** Perfect CSIR; ỹ = y·h*/max(|h|², ε_h) ≡ y/h for |h|² ≫ ε_h. After equalization the per-codeword SNR is |h|²P/σ² (instantaneous, heavy-tailed); the config SNR axis is the **average** SNR = P/σ² since E|h|² = 1. The identical equalizer is applied in the digital baseline. The guard keeps training gradients finite when |h| → 0.\\n+6. **SNR calculation & bandwidth ratio.** One function `snr_db → σ²` is the single source of truth for every method; no per-method recomputation, no E_b/N₀ on the comparison axis (digital-only supplementary label). Runtime asserts: ρ = k/6 with integer k, and n_dig == k for the digital chain (misconfiguration fails loudly rather than silently changing the budget).\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 5. FAIRNESS CHECK\\n+\\n+- **Single shared implementations** (not copies) of: dynamics, controller, normalization, channel models, equalizer, episode/RNG pipeline, metrics. A method can only differ in its encoder/quantizer → decoder/dequantizer map and its training objective.\\n+- **Identical for all three methods:** 6-D state; dynamics and limits; goal and success criterion; test episodes (same start/goal per episode index, frozen seeds); paired channel realizations (same n and h per episode/step); SNR grid and definition (P/σ² per complex symbol); P = 1; budget n_dig == k (asserted); 1 transmission per control step; perfect CSIR + ZF equalization; controller gains and clipping; horizon and metrics.\\n+- **Legitimately different (the independent variable):** how the state is mapped to channel symbols and back, and the training objective. The digital baseline may carry fewer effective source bits at matched k — that is a *result* (bandwidth-limited separation starves), not an unfairness, provided the budget equality holds and its configuration is reported.\\n+- **Guard rails in code:** runtime asserts (budget equality, shapes, identical seeds); an \\\"oracle perfect-state, no channel\\\" run allowed only as a clearly labeled upper reference, never a fourth comparator; normalization ranges from config only; no statistic ever computed on test data; digital BER/BLER reported as link diagnostics, never substituted for task metrics.\\n+\\n+**Decision A1 (digital budget), restated with options:**\\n+- **Option A — fit bits to budget:** for each ρ, choose (B, R_c, M) with 6B = k·R_c·log2(M), best feasible. Example feasible exact fits: k=3: uncoded 256-QAM → B=4 (≈1.07 m position quantization); uncoded 64-QAM → B=3; conv R_c=1/2 + 256-QAM → B=2. k=2: uncoded 64-QAM → B=2. k=1: B=1 at best — navigation-degenerate. Strictly matched, but the digital baseline is quantization-starved at ρ ≤ 1/2.\\n+- **Option B — scale budget to payload:** fix B = 8 (48 source bits), give the digital chain n_dig = ⌈48/(R_c·log2 M)⌉ symbols (e.g., 24 uncoded 256-QAM symbols, ρ_dig = 4; or 48 QPSK symbols with R_c = 1/2, ρ_dig = 8), and report its true bandwidth ratio alongside. Your protocol doc itself sketches this direction (16-bit example → k = 48).\\n+- **Recommendation:** run the main matrix at the frozen ρ ∈ {1/6, 1/3, 1/2} with Option-A digital configurations (fair at equal k, expected to fail — a genuine finding), **plus** Option-B digital reference curves clearly labeled with their larger ρ. This keeps budget-matched honesty and still shows what separated design achieves when given enough bandwidth. Your sign-off required.\\n+\\n+---\\n+\\n+## 6. IMPLEMENTATION RISKS (ways this could silently become mathematically inconsistent)\\n+\\n+1. **I/Q variance factor-2 bug** — sampling n_R, n_I with variance σ² instead of σ²/2 shifts every SNR by 3 dB. Mitigation: the §4.3 empirical test.\\n+2. **Channel-use miscounting** — treating 2k real outputs as 2k uses, or letting the digital chain use n_dig ≠ k without asserting it. Mitigation: runtime asserts + config sanity print.\\n+3. **Wrong normalization granularity** — per-symbol or per-batch power normalization instead of per-codeword changes the SNR semantics. Mitigation: per-sample check that (1/k)Σ|z_i|² = P.\\n+4. **Fast vs block fading** — drawing h per symbol instead of per codeword destroys the slow-fading comparison. Mitigation: h shape [B,1] and the correlation test in §4.4.\\n+5. **Asymmetric CSI** — equalizing one method and not another, or ε_h applied in only some paths. Mitigation: one shared equalizer module.\\n+6. **SNR-axis drift for digital** — quoting E_b/N₀ for the coded/modulated chain against E_s/N₀ for DeepJSCC. Mitigation: single σ² source of truth; E_b/N₀ only as a label.\\n+7. **Normalization leakage or drift** — ranges computed from data, or different clip behavior between train and eval; denormalization using unclipped bounds. Mitigation: constants in config, one pair of functions used everywhere.\\n+8. **Controller information leak** — feeding any ground-truth quantity (e.g., true goal or true position) to one method's controller. Every controller input must come from that method's received representation. Mitigation: controller consumes only the decoded/denormalized state tensor.\\n+9. **Autograd pitfalls in the rollout** — detaching z or h, or clipping away all gradient (dead zones at saturation are physically correct but must be understood); noise/h must enter as constants (leaves), while gradients flow through z, decoder, encoder. Mitigation: gradient-flow unit test (loss.backward reaches encoder weights).\\n+10. **Loss off-by-one** — Ld/Lv summed over the wrong index range, Lu including t = T, or LT evaluated at T−1. Mitigation: implement exactly as §1.1 row 12; one shared loss used for both training and reporting.\\n+11. **Success/failure semantics mismatch** — ∃t vs terminal-only success, and inconsistent boundary-exit handling between training and eval. Mitigation: A4/A5 frozen in config; one episode-termination module.\\n+12. **Digital strawman or capacity ghost** — accidentally giving the digital chain capacity-achieving performance, or crippling it via a coarse quantizer without reporting the budget arithmetic. Keep simple: required arg.\\n\\n```python\\ndef build_normalization_ranges(cfg: NormalizationConfig) -> torch.Tensor:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Row order: [x, y, vx, vy, x_g, y_g]; columns: (a_i, b_i). Shape [6, 2].\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    return torch.tensor(\\n        [cfg.position_range, cfg.position_range,\\n         cfg.velocity_range, cfg.velocity_range,\\n         cfg.goal_range, cfg.goal_range],\\n        dtype=torch.float32,\\n    )\\n\\n\\ndef normalize(s: torch.Tensor, ranges: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"[FROZEN] s_bar = 2(clip(s,a,b)-a)/(b-a)-1. s: [...,6], ranges: [6,2].\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    a = ranges[..., 0]\\n    b = ranges[..., 1]\\n    s_cl = torch.minimum(torch.maximum(s, a), b)\\n    return 2.0 * (s_cl - a) / (b - a) - 1.0\\n\\n\\ndef denormalize(s_bar: torch.Tensor, ranges: torch.Tensor, clip: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Exact inverse (clip=False). clip=True saturates to [a,b] (used only where\\n    a decoded state must be forced into range; it is enforced here as a norm clip inside the shared dynamics\\nso that every method (and the noiseless oracle) sees identical handling:\\n\\n    v_{t+1} = v_max * v_raw / ||v_raw||   if ||v_raw|| > v_max  else v_raw\\n\\nThis is differentiable almost everywhere (kink only at ||v_raw|| = v_max).\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"\\nfrom __future__ import annotations\\nimport torch\\nfrom project.config import UAVConfig\\n\\n\\ndef velocity_limit_clip(v: torch.Tensor, cfg: UAVConfig) -> torch.Tensor:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"[PROJ][A3] Scale v to unit norm * v_max whenever ||v|| > v_max.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    if not cfg.enforce_v_max:\\n        return v\\n    v_norm = torch.linalg.vector_norm(v, dim=-1, keepdim=True)\\n    scale = (cfg.v_max / v_norm.clamp_min(cfg.vel_clip_eps)).clamp(max=1.0)\\n    return v * scale\\n\\n\\ndef uav_step(p, v, u, cfg):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"One discrete dynamics step. p, v, u: [..., 2]. Differentiable.\\n    Noise/h must be attached elsewhere; this function only does arithmetic.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    dt = cfg.dt\\n    p_next = p + dt * v + 0.5 * (dt ** 2) * u\\n    v_raw = v + dt * u\\n    v_next = velocity_limit_clip(v_raw, cfg)\\n    return p_next, v_next\\n```\\n\\n--- controller.py ---\\n\\n```python\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"Fixed PD navigation controller shared by all three communication methods.\\n\\n    u_raw = -Kp (p - p_goal) - Kv v                [FROZEN]\\n    u     = clip(u_raw, -u_max, +u_max)            [FROZEN]\\n\\nThe controller is a PURE function of the state estimate passed to it. It reads\\nno globals and has no access to ground-truth state beyond its argument, so it\\ncan be fed a reconstructed/decoded estimate without any information leak\\n(audit risk #8).\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"\\nfrom __future__ import annotations\\nimport torch\\nfrom project.config import ControllerConfig\\n\\n\\ndef pd_controller(state_estimate: torch.Tensor, cfg: ControllerConfig) -> torch.Tensor:\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"state_estimate: [..., 6] = [x, y, vx, vy, x_g, y_g] (estimate, raw units).\\n    Returns u: [..., 2] within [-u_max, u_max]^2.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    p = state_estimate[..., 0:2]\\n    v = state_estimate[..., 2:4]\\n    p_goal = state_estimate[..., 4:6]\\n    u_raw = -cfg.Kp * (p - p_goal) - cfg.Kv * v\\n    return torch.clamp(u_raw, min=-cfg.u_max, max=cfg.u_max)\\n```\\n\\n--- environment.py ---\\n\\n```python\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"Minimal deterministic 2-D navigation environment (evaluation side).\\n\\nFrozen semantics (audit A4/A5):\\n* success  = 1[d_t <= r_g for some t in {0..T_max}]  (first hit counts)\\n* time_to_goal = first t with d_t <= r_g (None if never)\\n* final distance and minimum distance are separate quantities\\n* positions are NEVER clipped; leaving the workspace sets out_of_bounds and\\n  terminates the episode (a failure unless the goal was already reached)\\n* the velocity limit is enforced inside the shared dynamics ([A3])\\n* no obstacles, no collisions: the workspace boundary is the only constraint.\\n\\nTraining rollouts for task-oriented DeepJSCC (later steps) use\\nuav.dynamics.uav_step directly with a fixed horizon; they do not use this\\nclass, because early termination would break the uniform computation graph.\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"\\nfrom __future__ import annotations\\nfrom typing import Dict, Optional\\nimport torch\\nfrom project.config import Config\\nfrom project.uav.dynamics import uav_step\\n\\n\\nclass UAVNavigationEnv:\\n    def __init__(self, cfg: Config):\\n        self.cfg = cfg\\n\\n    # the winner and\\n+    its previous state are stored. (Note: a scatter over prev->next is\\n+    INVALID here because the map is 2-to-1 and scatter semantics for\\n+    duplicate indices are undefined.)\\n+\\n+    Traceback starts from state 0 (guaranteed by the zero tail); the\\n+    information bit at step t is the LSB of the next state (= the common\\n+    input u of both merged branches). 0].to(llrs.dtype)   # [64]\\n+    sign_a2 = 1.0 - 2.0 * out[prev_a, u_all, 1].to(llrs.dtype)\\n+    sign_b1 = 1.0 - 2.0 * out[prev_b, u_all, 0].to(llrs.dtype)\\n+    sign_b2 = 1.0 - 2.0 * out[prev_b, u_all, 1].to(llrs.dtype)\\n+\\n+    metrics = torch.full((B, 64), -1e30, device=device, dtype=llrs.dtype)\\n+    metrics[:, 0] = 0.0                               # start state 0\\n+    hist = []                                         # per-step winning prev\\n+    for t in range(L):\\n+        l1 = llrs[:, 2 * t].unsqueeze(1)              # [B, 1]\\n+        l2 = llrs[:, 2 * t + 1].unsqueeze(1)          # [B, 1]\\n+        bm_a = l1 * sign_a1.unsqueeze(0) + l2 * sign_a2.unsqueeze(0)  # [B, 64]\\n+        bm_b = l1 * sign_b1.unsqueeze(0) + l2 * sign_b2.unsqueeze(0)\\n+        c_a = metrics.gather(1, prev_a.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 64)) + bm_a\\n+        c_b = metrics.gather(1, prev_b.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 64)) + bm_b\\n+        take_b = c_b > c_a\\n+        metrics = torch.where(take_b, c_b, c_a)\\n+        hist.append(torch.where(take_b,\\n+                                prev_b.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 64),\\n+                                prev_a.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 64)))\\n+    # traceback from state 0; bit(t) = LSB of the next state\\n+    bits = llrs.new_zeros(B, L, dtype=torch.long)\\n+    state = torch.zeros(B, dtype=torch.long, of navigation-relevant information is a core requirement for autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operation over noisy and fading wireless links. Conventional digital communication systems and reconstruction-oriented Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (DeepJSCC) schemes are optimized to recover the transmitted signal with minimum distortion, independent of how that signal will subsequently be used. This project investigates a Task-Oriented DeepJSCC communication system in which the encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end to directly optimize UAV navigation (goal-reaching) performance rather than reconstruction fidelity.\\n25:A structured literature verification (Section 7) confirms that task-oriented and semantic communication has already been investigated for UAV command-and-control transmission, UAV swarm tracking control, and UAV vision-based localization, and that task-oriented DeepJSCC trained directly against a closed-loop control objective has been demonstrated for autonomous driving. The specific combination targeted here � a DeepJSCC encoder/decoder trained on a UAV navigation/goal-reaching objective, operating on a low-dimensional kinematic state rather than imagery, and systematically evaluated under both AWGN and Rayleigh fading against conventional and reconstruction-oriented baselines � has not been reported in the reviewed literature and forms the focus of this Final Year Project. The expected outcome is an empirically grounded characterization of when, and by how much, task-oriented optimization improves UAV navigation robustness relative to conventional and reconstruction-oriented alternatives under wireless channel impairments.\\n28:Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (DeepJSCC) replaces the separate source and channel coding stages with a pair of jointly trained neural networks that map source symbols directly to complex-valued channel input symbols, and has been shown both under AWGN and slow Rayleigh fading to degrade gracefully rather than catastrophically as SNR deteriorates (Bourtsoulatze, Kurka & G�nd�z, 2019). The great majority of DeepJSCC research, however, is reconstruction-oriented: the encoder and decoder are trained to minimize a distortion metric between the transmitted and received signal, independent of what the received information will subsequently be used for. In parallel, a body of work on task-oriented and goal-oriented communication argues that when the purpose of transmission is a downstream decision or control action, the communication system should instead be optimized directly against that downstream task's performance rather than against signal fidelity (G�nd�z et al., 2023; Shao, Mao & Zhang, 2022).\\n29:This project investigates the intersection of these two ideas for a specific and practically relevant downstream task: UAV navigation toward a goal position. It asks whether training a DeepJSCC encoder/decoder pair directly on navigation/goal-reaching performance, rather than on reconstruction error, yields a communication system that is more robust to wireless channel impairments in the sense that matters to the mission � reaching the goal � even if it is not necessarily better at reproducing the original navigation state bit-for-bit.\\n34:Classical digital communication systems follow Shannon's source-channel separation principle: a source coder compresses the data and a channel coder adds redundancy for error protection, with the two designed independently. While asymptotically optimal for point-to-point channels with unbounded blocklength, separation-based systems are known to perform poorly at short blocklengths and to fail abruptly when the operating SNR drops below the design point. DeepJSCC instead parameterizes the encoder and decoder as convolutional or transformer-based neural networks trained end-to-end as an autoencoder, with a non-trainable channel layer inserted between them to model the wireless channel (Bourtsoulatze, Kurka & G�nd�z, 2019). Subsequent work has extended DeepJSCC with attention modules for content-adaptive coding (Xu et al., 2022), bandwidth-agile and variable-rate transmission (Kurka & G�nd�z, 2021), and explicit multipath/fading and MIMO channel models (Yang, Bian & Kim, 2022; Wu et al., 2024).\\n37:A Task-Oriented DeepJSCC system, as investigated in this project, combines both ideas: it uses the DeepJSCC architecture (a jointly trained neural encoder/decoder mapping directly to channel symbols, without explicit source/channel separation) but replaces the reconstruction-based training objective with a task-oriented loss defined on the downstream task's performance.\\n39:UAV communication links differ from static or slowly moving terrestrial links in that the channel can vary rapidly due to the UAV's own motion, altitude changes, and antenna orientation, producing time-varying multipath and Doppler effects. Bandwidth is also often constrained by regulatory allocation and by the need to share spectrum with other aerial or ground users. These characteristics motivate the choice of AWGN and Rayleigh fading as the two channel models investigated in this project: AWGN represents a noise-limited baseline case, while Rayleigh fading represents a non-line-of-sight, richly scattering environment representative of low-altitude urban or cluttered operation.\\n43:When a UAV's navigation-relevant state information (position, velocity, and goal information) is transmitted over a noisy or fading wireless channel using either a conventional digital pipeline or a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC scheme, the communication system is optimized to minimize a generic distortion measure on the transmitted state vector. This measure does not necessarily correspond to what matters operationally: the UAV's ability to reach its goal safely and efficiently. Under a fixed bandwidth and SNR budget, a communication system that spends its limited channel-use budget reproducing every component of the state vector with equal fidelity may perform worse, in terms of navigation outcome, than a system that allocates its representational capacity toward the state information that is most relevant to the navigation decision. The problem addressed in this project is therefore whether, and to what extent, training a DeepJSCC encoder/decoder directly against a navigation-task objective � a Task-Oriented DeepJSCC system � improves UAV navigation performance relative to conventional digital communication and reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC, under identical AWGN and Rayleigh fading channel conditions.\\n45:From a communications engineering perspective, this project is motivated by three considerations. First, UAV platforms are typically bandwidth- and power-constrained, so any reduction in the channel resources needed to achieve a given navigation reliability is operationally valuable. Second, the graceful-degradation property already demonstrated for reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC under AWGN and Rayleigh fading (Bourtsoulatze, Kurka & G�nd�z, 2019) suggests that a task-oriented variant may inherit similar robustness while additionally concentrating representational capacity on task-relevant information, potentially widening the performance gap over conventional digital transmission at low SNR. Third, while task-oriented DeepJSCC has already been shown to improve closed-loop control task performance under noisy channels in the autonomous-driving domain (Diao et al., 2024, 2025), it has not been evaluated for UAV navigation using a compact kinematic state representation, leaving open whether the same benefits transfer to a lower-dimensional, non-visual source and to a mobile aerial channel environment.\\n49:Bourtsoulatze, Kurka and G�nd�z (2019) introduced DeepJSCC for wireless image transmission, showing that a jointly trained convolutional encoder/decoder mapping pixel values directly to channel symbols outperforms JPEG/JPEG2000-plus-capacity-achieving-channel-coding baselines at low SNR and small bandwidth, avoids the cliff effect under AWGN, and, under slow Rayleigh fading, learns fading-resilient representations that significantly outperform separation-based digital transmission at all tested SNR and bandwidth values. This paper establishes both the DeepJSCC architecture and the AWGN/Rayleigh evaluation protocol adopted in this project. Subsequent works extended the architecture with attention modules for content/channel-adaptive coding (Xu et al., 2022), variable-rate and bandwidth-agile coding (Kurka & G�nd�z, 2021), explicit OFDM-based multipath fading channels (Yang, Bian & Kim, 2022), and MIMO fading channels (Wu et al., 2024). These works confirm that channel-aware DeepJSCC under AWGN and Rayleigh (and richer fading models) is a mature, well-validated methodology, but remain reconstruction-oriented: the training objective is signal fidelity (e.g., mean-squared error or a perceptual metric), not a downstream task outcome.\\n53:Several papers apply semantic or task-oriented ideas specifically to UAVs, but none trains a DeepJSCC-style neural channel-symbol encoder directly against a navigation/goal-reaching objective. Xu, Zhou and Deng (2023) propose a task-oriented semantics-aware (TOSA) framework for UAV command-and-control (C&C) transmission that defines the value of information using similarity and age-of-information metrics; this addresses scheduling and importance-weighting of C&C messages rather than learning a joint source-channel neural code. Wu, Yang, Deng and Aghvami (2024) propose goal-oriented semantic communication for robotic (including UAV) waypoint transmission, using a deep reinforcement learning agent to generate optimal C&C data and a proactive repetition scheme (DeepPro) to combat channel unreliability; again, this is a scheduling/repetition strategy layered on generated commands rather than a trained DeepJSCC encoder/decoder. Tang, Feng and Quek (2024, 2025) study decentralized semantic communication and cooperative tracking control for a UAV swarm over MIMO fading channels, using a semantic triggering rule (whether to transmit at all, based on tracking-error cost and channel state) combined with a Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty control law; this addresses when to transmit, not how to jointly encode the state into channel symbols. Fang et al. (2025) propose a task-oriented communication framework for UAV visual localization/navigation in GPS-denied environments, using an orthogonally-constrained variational information bottleneck (O-VIB) encoder to compress multi-camera image features before transmission to an edge server for position estimation; the wireless link here is modeled through a Shannon-capacity/rate expression incorporating path loss, shadowing, and small-scale fading as a scalar channel gain, rather than as a differentiable, symbol-level AWGN/Rayleigh channel embedded directly in end-to-end training, and the task is position estimation (localization) rather than closed-loop goal-reaching control.\\n55:The methodologically closest precedent to this project is a series of papers by Diao and colleagues on task-oriented source-channel coding for autonomous driving. Diao, Meng, Xu, She and Zhao (2024) propose a Task-oriented Source-Channel Coding (TSCC) framework that uses a modified conditional variational autoencoder guided by an autonomous-driving agent to jointly optimize source and channel coding, tested under different communication channel conditions on a driving simulator. Diao, Zhang, De Martini, Zhao and Li (2025) extend this to a task-oriented co-design of communication, computing, and control for industrial cyber-physical systems, combining a VIB-based task-oriented JSCC with a delay-aware control-prediction strategy, reporting large bandwidth reductions with maintained driving performance under low-SNR conditions in the CARLA simulator. A related paper, Diao, Zhang, She, Zhao and Li (2025), proposes an alignment between task-oriented and reconstruction-oriented communication for edge intelligence, and the associated doctoral thesis (Diao, 2025) consolidates this line of work, explicitly reporting large communication-bandwidth reductions while maintaining driving performance under noisy channels. This body of work demonstrates conclusively that a DeepJSCC-style, end-to-end-trained system optimized directly against closed-loop control-task performance under a noisy channel is both feasible and beneficial � but exclusively for ground-vehicle autonomous driving using camera imagery as the source, not for UAV navigation using a compact kinematic state vector, and without a systematic, matched-bandwidth comparison across both AWGN and Rayleigh fading of the kind proposed here.\\n85:No neural joint source-channel encoder; not navigation-outcome trained\\n99:Scheduling/triggering, not a trained channel-symbol codec\\n109:Task-oriented JSCC (CVAE/VIB) trained on control task\\n===audit-2.6===\\n55-- **A5 — Boundary-exit / failure semantics.** Leaving the workspace must terminate eval episodes (counted as failure). ((out - s * 0.0) ** 2).mean()\\n+                optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)\\n+                loss.backward()\\n+                torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(),\\n+                                               max_norm=config.GRAD_CLIP_NORM)\\n+                optimizer.step()\\n+                losses.append(float(loss))\\n+            return losses\\n+\\n+    and all(torch.equal(a[\\\"exp_avg\\\"], b[\\\"exp_avg\\\"])\\n+                      and torch.equal(a[\\\"exp_avg_sq\\\"], b[\\\"exp_avg_sq\\\"])\\n+                      and a[\\\"step\\\"] ==    cont_a = segment(m1, opt, gen, 30)\\n+\\n+        # --- continuation arm B: FULL RNG state (global + data generator) ---\\n+        gen_b.set_state(torch.load(gen_state_path))\\n+        cont_b = Does task-oriented JSCC improve when the objective better reflects the control problem? This isolates whether the failure is fundamental or a loss-shaping artifact.\\n•\\tArchitecture Ablation: Your MLP is small. Test a larger network or a different architecture (e.g., residual connections, attention). This rules out the criticism that the failure is due to insufficient model capacity.\\n•\\tObjective Ablation: Compare your distance-based task loss against a \\\"task-aware\\\" reconstruction loss (e.g., weighted MSE that prioritizes position over velocity). This tests the hypothesis that reconstruction is inherently better for this task.\\n2. Investigate Training Instability\\nFigure 10 in your results shows alarming oscillation in the task loss. You must diagnose this.\\n•\\tAction: Run the k=24, seed 42 task training with multiple random initializations and track the loss trajectory. Your negative result provides the motivation for this.\\n•\\tProposed Contribution: Develop an Aligned Task- and Reconstruction-Oriented (ATROC) JSCC framework . The idea is to use a reconstruction-oriented encoder but introduce a lightweight \\\"information reshaper\\\" or task-specific decoder that transforms the reconstructed state into a control-optimal representation.\\n•\\tWhy this works: It preserves the robustness of reconstruction while allowing the task to guide the final stages. But frontier research is moving toward rateless transmission: coding can adaptively continue sending until the receiver \\\"recovers enough\\\" task-relevant information. This forms a natural complement to your finding that \\\"task-oriented fails under fixed bandwidth.\\\"\\nConcrete approach: Design a rateless DeepJSCC scheme where the UAV dynamically decides \\\"how many more symbols to send\\\" based on feedback about task execution success probability. The core novelty is: optimizing not reconstruction quality, but the minimal transmission amount needed for \\\"control task success\\\". This directly addresses the weak task signal problem in your current work—the rateless mechanism lets the model learn \\\"when stopping transmission is sufficient\\\" during training.\\nNovelty argument: Existing rateless JSCC work (e.g., the RLACS scheme from arXiv 2025) primarily targets image reconstruction tasks, and no work has applied rateless mechanisms to closed-loop control tasks. Your UAV navigation scenario is naturally suited for this extension.\\nDirection 2: Replace Immediate Distance with \\\"Causal Information Value\\\" as Reward (Strongest Theoretical Depth)\\nYour current task loss is myopic: distance penalty at each step + terminal distance. But control task value is long-horizon—a state token transmitted now may affect control effectiveness for dozens of steps into the future. Frontier work has proposed Causal Information Value (CIV): measuring the causal contribution of each transmitted semantic token to long-term return.\\nConcrete approach: Formulate the semantic communication problem as a \\\"long-term return per bit maximization\\\" problem. Instead of asking \\\"how accurately is this state reconstructed,\\\" ask \\\"does transmitting this state token causally improve the probability of future control success.\\\" This requires introducing a world model to imagine future trajectories, thereby estimating CIV. The WM-CDT framework has been validated in AirSim-Sionna UAV navigation tasks, where CIV aligns better with true long-term returns than myopic VoI, saliency, or confidence scores.\\nNovelty argument: CIV has been used in closed-loop physical AI systems for UAV navigation, but has not been combined with DeepJSCC transmission mechanisms. Your contribution could be: proving that under bandwidth-constrained DeepJSCC, CIV-guided token selection improves task success rates more than distance-loss-guided reconstruction. This directly addresses why your \\\"task-oriented approach failed\\\"—because the loss signal is myopic, not because task orientation itself is flawed.\\nDirection 3: Replace Uniform JSCC with \\\"Semantic Importance Non-Uniform Protection\\\" (Moderate Difficulty)\\nYour current task-oriented method treats all 6 state dimensions equally, but in control tasks, position matters more than velocity, terminal distance matters more than historical distance. Frontier work is exploring non-uniform error protection (UEP): allocating more transmission power or more reliable coding to task-critical features.\\nConcrete approach: Design a pyramid-style encoder (or lightweight attention mechanism) that decomposes the 6-D state into \\\"task-critical sub-features\\\" and \\\"task-secondary sub-features,\\\" then applies stronger channel protection to critical sub-features. Your current finding that \\\"task-oriented loss has λ_u = λ_v = 0\\\" already implies position information dominates the task—formalize this intuition into a learnable UEP mechanism.\\nNovelty argument: UEP-DeepJSCC has been proposed for image semantic transmission through a dual-priority framework of message importance and feature importance. But no work has applied it to low-dimensional control states. Your contribution could be: proving that in 6-D control tasks, UEP gains are more significant than in image tasks (because dimensionality is low, importance differences are more concentrated).\\nDirection 4: Turn \\\"Failure\\\" into a \\\"Theoretical Boundary\\\"\\nYour current work essentially discovers a boundary experimentally: when ρ ≤ 1/2, task-oriented JSCC underperforms reconstruction-oriented; when ρ ≥ 2, digital methods overtake. This boundary can be formalized information-theoretically.\\nConcrete approach: Derive a rate-distortion function for control tasks, defining \\\"control distortion\\\" not as state reconstruction error, but as the minimum mutual information required for task success. Semantic rate-distortion functions have been characterized as optimization problems simultaneously considering semantic distortion and observation distortion. Then use this boundary to explain why your experiments observed the crossover point.\\nNovelty argument: This is a theoretical contribution, particularly attractive to IEEE Transactions. No closed loop: isolates the receiver-side effect.\\n+\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n+import sys\\n+from pathlib import Path\\n+\\n+sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))\\n+\\n+import torch\\n+\\n+from project import config\\n+from project.baselines.digital import (DigitalBaseline, dequantize, qpsk_llrs,\\n+                                       pack_bits, quantize, unpack_bits,\\n+                                       viterbi_decode)\\n+from project.channels.rayleigh import equalize_zf, rayleigh_channel\\n+from project.data.normalization import normalize\\n+from project.uav.environment import NavigationEnv\\n+\\n+\\n+def ber_at(k, snr, sigma, episodes=4000):\\n+    B = config.DIGITAL_B_BY_K[k]\\n+    base = DigitalBaseline(k=k, bits_per_component=B)\\n+    env = NavigationEnv()\\n+    g = config.derive_generator(\\\"episodes\\\", config.TEST_SEED)\\n+    p0, v0, goal = env.sample_starts(episodes, generator=g)\\n+    g_noise = config.derive_generator(\\\"noise_test\\\", config.TEST_SEED)\\n+    sigma2 = config.TX_POWER * (10.0 ** (-snr / 10.0))\\n+    n = torch.complex(\\n+        torch.randn(episodes, k, generator=g_noise) * (sigma2 / 2.0) ** 0.5,\\n+        torch.randn(episodes, k, generator=g_noise) * (sigma2 / 2.0) ** 0.5)\\n+    h = torch.complex(torch.randn(episodes, 1, generator=g_noise) * 0.5 ** 0.5,\\n+                      torch.randn(episodes, 1, generator=g_noise) * 0.5 ** 0.5)\\n+    # Conventional Digital Communication Baseline\n\nThey must be evaluated under:\n\n* AWGN channel\n* Rayleigh fading channel\n\nThe comparison must use matched:\n\n* UAV environment\n* source state\n* channel conditions\n* SNR\n* bandwidth ratio\n* controller\n* test episodes\n* evaluation procedure\n\nThe primary task is UAV goal reaching.\n\n==================================================\nFROZEN UAV STATE\n================\n\nUse the 6-dimensional state:\n\ns_t = [x_t, y_t, vx_t, vy_t, x_g, y_g]^T ∈ R^6\n\nwhere:\n\nx_t, y_t       = UAV position\nvx_t, vy_t     = UAV velocity\nx_g, y_g       = goal position\n\nDo not change this state representation unless I explicitly ask.\n\n==================================================\nFROZEN UAV DYNAMICS\n===================\n\nUse the 2D double-integrator:\n\np_t = [x_t, y_t]^T\nv_t = [vx_t, vy_t]^T\nu_t = [ax_t, ay_t]^T\n\np_{t+1} = p_t + dt*v_t + 0.5*dt^2*u_t\n\nv_{t+1} = v_t + dt*u_t\n\nThe dynamics must be implemented as a differentiable PyTorch operation where required for task-oriented training.\n\n==================================================\nGOAL AND SUCCESS\n================\n\nGoal:\n\np_g = [x_g, y_g]^T\n\nPosition error:\n\ne_t = p_t - {"id": "961ac1fb-8b69-475f-9d2b-041c8ce756f1", "thread_id": "c4fec73a-5e9f-45ed-839c-075dc0c49a5e", "kind": "prompt", "prompt": "This research is trying to figure out the best way to send information from a drone to itself (or to a controller) over a noisy, unreliable radio link so the drone can still navigate to a target. Normally, when you send data over a bad connection, you first compress it, then add error-correction bits, then transmit—and if some bits get corrupted, the drone's position estimate goes wrong and it crashes or misses the goal. This project instead tests a smarter approach called \"task-oriented joint source-channel coding,\" where a neural network learns to encode the drone's state (position, velocity, goal) directly into radio symbols in a way that's optimized not for perfect reconstruction of the data, but for the actual task—reaching the goal. They compare three methods: (1) a traditional digital baseline that quantizes, adds convolutional codes, and uses QPSK (the \"old-school\" way), (2) a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC that tries to faithfully rebuild the drone's state at the receiver, and (3) a task-oriented DeepJSCC that skips caring about perfect reconstruction and directly minimizes navigation error. They test all three under different bandwidths (how many radio symbols you're allowed to use per state update) and different noise levels, in both clean AWGN channels and fading Rayleigh channels. The surprising finding is that the fancy task-oriented neural approach actually does worse than plain reconstruction at low bandwidth, and the traditional digital method wins big once you give it enough bandwidth—so the \"task-oriented\" idea isn't automatically better; it depends on how much radio spectrum you have. {"text": "Achha sawal — simple language mein samjhata hoon, aapke hi project ke numbers ke sath:\n\n## Batch processing kya hai?\nModel ek baar mein **ek example** pe seekh sakta tha (slow + noisy), lekin hum **ek saath hazaron examples** ka bundle (\"batch\") dete hain. Us poore bundle ka average error nikaal kar ek gradient step lagti hai. Isi ko batch training kehte hain.\n\n## Aapke project mein exactly kya ho raha hai\n\n**Reconstruction training (batch = 4096 states):**\n- Har step pe model ko **4096 alag state vectors** (UAV position/velocity) ek saath diye jate hain\n- Encoder in sab ko compress karta hai (k symbols), channel se guzarta hai, decoder reconstruct karta hai\n- Sab 4096 ka **average MSE loss** → ek Adam step\n- Itne bade batch se loss estimate **stable** hota hai (kam noise) — is liye 5000 steps mein model saaf seekh jata hai\n\n**Task training (batch = 256 episodes × T=100 steps):**\n- Yahan \"example\" = ek **pura navigation episode** (100 time steps ka rollout)\n- Har step pe PD controller → transmission → decoder → next state — poora trajectory\n- 256 episodes parallel roll out hote hain, sab ka combined task loss (distance + terminal penalty) → ek gradient step\n- Har episode ka **alag random start/goal/noise** hota hai — batch mein variety aati hai\n\n## Batch kyun zaroori hai? (3 wajahain)\n\n1. **Speed:** CPU/GPU vectorized operations hazaaron examples pe ek sath chalte hain — 4096 states ka ek forward pass, 4096 alag-alag passes se hazaron guna tez hai. Isi liye aapka recon run sirf ~2 min leta hai.\n2. **Stable gradients:** Ek example ka gradient bohat noisy hota hai (kabhi bohat bara, kabhi zero) — training uchhalti rehti hai. Batch average se smooth signal milta hai, isi liye Adam lr=1e-3 pe convergence clean hai.\n3. **Fair comparison:** Frozen batch sizes (4096/256) ka matlab — **task aur reconstruction dono ne bilkul same conditions mein seekha**. Yehi aapke experimental protocol ki credibility hai (Step 9C mein frozen kiya tha).\n\n## Ek important farq (jo report mein bhi aata hai)\n- **Training batch** (256/4096) = seekhne ki unit\n- **Eval episodes** (5000) = final exam ki unit — yahan batching sirf speed ke liye hai, success rate ka **reliable statistics** (Wilson CI) nikalne ke liye 5000 chahiye\n\nMatlab: batch processing koi \"extra feature\" nahi — wo hi hai jo 60 training runs ko aaj complete karna mumkin banata hai, aur frozen values hi task-vs-recon ko fair banati hain.\n", "thread_id": "58285251-b77f-4ee9-b493-5b63c150436b"}

{"text": "This research is trying to figure out the best way to send information from a drone to itself (or to a controller) over a noisy, unreliable radio link so the drone can still navigate to a target. Normally, when you send data over a bad connection, you first compress it, then add error-correction bits, then transmit—and if some bits get corrupted, the drone's position estimate goes wrong and it crashes or misses the goal. This project instead tests a smarter approach called \"task-oriented joint source-channel coding,\" where a neural network learns to encode the drone's state (position, velocity, goal) directly into radio symbols in a way that's optimized not for perfect reconstruction of the data, but for the actual task—reaching the goal. They compare three methods: (1) a traditional digital baseline that quantizes, adds convolutional codes, and uses QPSK (the \"old-school\" way), (2) a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC that tries to faithfully rebuild the drone's state at the receiver, and (3) a task-oriented DeepJSCC that skips caring about perfect reconstruction and directly minimizes navigation error. They test all three under different bandwidths (how many radio symbols you're allowed to use per state update) and different noise levels, in both clean AWGN channels and fading Rayleigh channels. The surprising finding is that the fancy task-oriented neural approach actually does worse than plain reconstruction at low bandwidth, and the traditional digital method wins big once you give it enough bandwidth—so the \"task-oriented\" idea isn't automatically better; it depends on how much radio spectrum you have. The whole thing is built as a rigorous, reproducible experiment with frozen settings, multiple random seeds, and proper statistics, so the comparisons are fair and not cherry-picked.\n\n Mam Ismat: Novelty pr question hai\n Mam Ismat: Or research question mein msla hai\n Mam Ismat: UAV khud ko hi message send kr ra\n\nmam ka view hai\n", "thread_id": "c4fec73a-5e9f-45ed-839c-075dc0c49a5e"}

{"text": "This research is trying to figure out the best way to send information from a drone to itself (or to a controller) over a noisy, unreliable radio link so the drone can still navigate to a target. Normally, when you send data over a bad connection, you first compress it, then add error-correction bits, then transmit—and if some bits get corrupted, the drone's position estimate goes wrong and it crashes or misses the goal. This project instead tests a smarter approach called \"task-oriented joint source-channel coding,\" where a neural network learns to encode the drone's state (position, velocity, goal) directly into radio symbols in a way that's optimized not for perfect reconstruction of the data, but for the actual task—reaching the goal. They compare three methods: (1) a traditional digital baseline that quantizes, adds convolutional codes, and uses QPSK (the \"old-school\" way), (2) a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC that tries to faithfully rebuild the drone's state at the receiver, and (3) a task-oriented DeepJSCC that skips caring about perfect reconstruction and directly minimizes navigation error. They test all three under different bandwidths (how many radio symbols you're allowed to use per state update) and different noise levels, in both clean AWGN channels and fading Rayleigh channels. The surprising finding is that the fancy task-oriented neural approach actually does worse than plain reconstruction at low bandwidth, and the traditional digital method wins big once you give it enough bandwidth—so the \"task-oriented\" idea isn't automatically better; it depends on how much radio spectrum you have. {"id": 126, "c0": "Achha sawal — simple language mein samjhata hoon, aapke hi project ke numbers ke sath:\n\n## Batch processing kya hai?\nModel ek baar mein **ek example** pe seekh sakta tha (slow + noisy), lekin hum **ek saath hazaron examples** ka bundle (\"batch\") dete hain. Us poore bundle ka average error nikaal kar ek gradient step lagti hai. Isi ko batch training kehte hain.\n\n## Aapke project mein exactly kya ho raha hai\n\n**Reconstruction training (batch = 4096 states):**\n- Har step pe model ko **4096 alag state vectors** (UAV position/velocity) ek saath diye jate hain\n- Encoder in sab ko compress karta hai (k symbols), channel se guzarta hai, decoder reconstruct karta hai\n- Sab 4096 ka **average MSE loss** → ek Adam step\n- Itne bade batch se loss estimate **stable** hota hai (kam noise) — is liye 5000 steps mein model saaf seekh jata hai\n\n**Task training (batch = 256 episodes × T=100 steps):**\n- Yahan \"example\" = ek **pura navigation episode** (100 time steps ka rollout)\n- Har step pe PD controller → transmission → decoder → next state — poora trajectory\n- 256 episodes parallel roll out hote hain, sab ka combined task loss (distance + terminal penalty) → ek gradient step\n- Har episode ka **alag random start/goal/noise** hota hai — batch mein variety aati hai\n\n## Batch kyun zaroori hai? (3 wajahain)\n\n1. **Speed:** CPU/GPU vectorized operations hazaaron examples pe ek sath chalte hain — 4096 states ka ek forward pass, 4096 alag-alag passes se hazaron guna tez hai. Isi liye aapka recon run sirf ~2 min leta hai.\n2. **Stable gradients:** Ek example ka gradient bohat noisy hota hai (kabhi bohat bara, kabhi zero) — training uchhalti rehti hai. Batch average se smooth signal milta hai, isi liye Adam lr=1e-3 pe convergence clean hai.\n3. **Fair comparison:** Frozen batch sizes (4096/256) ka matlab — **task aur reconstruction dono ne bilkul same conditions mein seekha**. Yehi aapke experimental protocol ki credibility hai (Step 9C mein frozen kiya tha).\n\n## Ek important farq (jo report mein bhi aata hai)\n- **Training batch** (256/4096) = seekhne ki unit\n- **Eval episodes** (5000) = final exam ki unit — yahan batching sirf speed ke liye hai, success rate ka **reliable statistics** (Wilson CI) nikalne ke liye 5000 chahiye\n\nMatlab: batch processing koi \"extra feature\" nahi — wo hi hai jo 60 training runs ko aaj complete karna mumkin banata hai, aur frozen values hi task-vs-recon ko fair banati hain.\n", "c1": "58285251-b77f-4ee9-b493-5b63c150436b"}

{"id": 241, "c0": "This research is trying to figure out the best way to send information from a drone to itself (or to a controller) over a noisy, unreliable radio link so the drone can still navigate to a target. Normally, when you send data over a bad connection, you first compress it, then add error-correction bits, then transmit—and if some bits get corrupted, the drone's position estimate goes wrong and it crashes or misses the goal. This project instead tests a smarter approach called \"task-oriented joint source-channel coding,\" where a neural network learns to encode the drone's state (position, velocity, goal) directly into radio symbols in a way that's optimized not for perfect reconstruction of the data, but for the actual task—reaching the goal. They compare three methods: (1) a traditional digital baseline that quantizes, adds convolutional codes, and uses QPSK (the \"old-school\" way), (2) a reconstruction-oriented DeepJSCC that tries to faithfully rebuild the drone's state at the receiver, and (3) a task-oriented DeepJSCC that skips caring about perfect reconstruction and directly minimizes navigation error. They test all three under different bandwidths (how many radio symbols you're allowed to use per state update) and different noise levels, in both clean AWGN channels and fading Rayleigh channels. The surprising finding is that the fancy task-oriented neural approach actually does worse than plain reconstruction at low bandwidth, and the traditional digital method wins big once you give it enough bandwidth—so the \"task-oriented\" idea isn't automatically better; it depends on how much radio spectrum you have. The whole thing is built as a rigorous, reproducible experiment with frozen settings, multiple random seeds, and proper statistics, so the comparisons are fair and not cherry-picked.\n\n Mam Ismat: Novelty pr question hai\n Mam Ismat: Or research question mein msla hai\n Mam Ismat: UAV khud ko hi message send kr ra\n\nmam ka view hai\n", "c1": "c4fec73a-5e9f-45ed-839c-075dc0c49a5e"}
